title: The Megaprojects That Even the Ancient Romans Couldn’t Pull Off: Rerouting the Tiber, Digging a Canal, and More
description:

body:
in History |   	October 15th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Some would call the Unit­ed States of Amer­i­ca the might­i­est empire the world has ever known. Yet over the past half-cen­tu­ry or so, it has shown a strange inabil­i­ty to build domes­tic infra­struc­ture, at least at the effi­cien­cy or on the scale seen else­where in the world. (This will not come as news to Amer­i­can enthu­si­asts of high-speed rail.) Here on Open Cul­ture, we’ve pre­vi­ous­ly fea­tured his­to­ry YouTu­ber Gar­rett Ryan’s take on the ques­tion of whether the U.S. is now declin­ing like the ancient Roman Empire. On a more recent video for his chan­nel Told in Stone, he’s high­light­ed the megapro­jects that even the Romans — who man­aged the Pan­theon, the Colos­se­um, and the Pont du Gard, to say noth­ing of their unique­ly long-last­ing con­crete itself — could­n’t pull off.
The Tiber may seem like a tame riv­er today, but it was­n’t always so placid. In antiq­ui­ty, rains caused it to flood every year. Sen­a­tor-his­to­ri­an Cas­sius Dio record­ed an inci­dent in 54 BC when the sud­den­ly ris­ing waters caused not just hous­es but whole neigh­bor­hoods to col­lapse. The Tiber’s flood­ing wors­ened over time, inspir­ing Julius Cae­sar to pro­pose re-rout­ing it either around Rome or into a tun­nel run­ning beneath the city. Unfor­tu­nate­ly, the Ides of March came before work could get under­way. Augus­tus opt­ed to dredge the riv­er chan­nel, and Tiberius cham­pi­oned divert­ing its trib­u­taries. Only the con­struc­tion of mod­ern embank­ments in the nine­teenth cen­tu­ry brought the reg­u­lar flu­vial dis­as­ters under con­trol, ensur­ing peace for strollers in search of their own dolce vita.
Roman ships sail­ing to Greece had to make their way around the Pelo­pon­nese, the south of the Greek penin­su­la. The dan­gers of that stretch were many, and did their part to sink the ship car­ry­ing the Antikythera Mech­a­nism. The Isth­mus of Corinth held out the promise of safer pas­sage, at least for those will­ing to drag their laden ships over a bit of land. Dig­ging a canal was, in some sense, the obvi­ous solu­tion, con­sid­ered by both Julius Cae­sar and Caligu­la, but “only Nero was mega­lo­ma­ni­a­cal enough to actu­al­ly begin the project.” A decent amount of progress had been made before anoth­er instance of regi­cide (or per­haps, in this par­tic­u­lar case, tyran­ni­cide) put a stop to the work. Rather than being resumed by a lat­er emper­or, the canal “became a byword for hubris” — at least until the job was final­ly done in the uncom­mon­ly ambi­tious nine­teenth cen­tu­ry.
In cen­tral Ger­many, near where the vil­lage of Wald­girmes is today, Romans found­ed a city with many fea­tures of an impe­r­i­al set­tle­ment, such as a clas­sic street grid, pipes run­ning from a cen­tral aque­duct, and a forum, at the cen­ter of which a gild­ed stat­ue of Augus­tus on horse­back once stood. Dat­ing to the year 4 BC, the city was intend­ed as a new cap­i­tal for what the Romans called Ger­ma­nia, though it end­ed up aban­doned after the Bat­tle of the Teu­to­burg For­est only about a decade after its found­ing. “The build­ings were burned,” Ryan says. “The head of Augus­tus’ eques­tri­an stat­ue was thrown down a well,” only to be dis­cov­ered nine­teen cen­turies lat­er. That image could inspire a med­i­ta­tion on what may be the way of all empires — or serve as a warn­ing to any Amer­i­can leader con­sid­er­ing immor­tal­iz­ing him­self and his horse in gold.

title: How Vincent van Gogh’s Sister-in-Law Worked Tirelessly to Make Him Famous
description:
in Art, History |   	October 16th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

No artist, no mat­ter how soli­tary by nature, becomes a cul­tur­al phe­nom­e­non
body:
in Art, History |   	October 16th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

No artist, no mat­ter how soli­tary by nature, becomes a cul­tur­al phe­nom­e­non alone. That’s even true of such an iso­lat­ed fig­ure as Vin­cent van Gogh, whose death in obscu­ri­ty at the age of 37 left open the ques­tion of who, if any­one, would vouch­safe his paint­ings to pos­ter­i­ty. The sup­port of the artist’s younger broth­er Theo is often giv­en a good deal of cred­it for mak­ing his work pos­si­ble, and not with­out rea­son. What’s some­what less wide­ly known is that Theo, who’d long been in poor health, died less than a year after Vin­cen­t’s sui­cide. The work of ensur­ing the lat­ter’s lega­cy then fell to the for­mer’s wid­ow Johan­na Bonger — or per­haps she under­stood that if she did­n’t stew­ard it, nobody else would.
As Cindy Poh explains in the New­s­think video above, Bonger inher­it­ed a great many of van Gogh’s works and stored them away while devis­ing a plan to make them famous. Prac­ti­cal­ly going door-to-door — and some­times, it seems, lit­er­al­ly going door-to-door — she stayed engaged with the late Theo’s art-world con­tacts. She cut sweet­heart deals with muse­ums and even donat­ed art­works out­right, increas­ing their chance of pub­lic expo­sure. She orga­nized exhi­bi­tions every­where from Paris to Berlin to Lon­don to New York, the most piv­otal being one held at Ams­ter­dam’s Stedelijk Muse­um in 1905. The 484 works put on dis­play made it the largest van Gogh show in his­to­ry, a record it still holds today.


	

At that time, well before The Star­ry Night and Sun­flow­ers adorned cof­fee mugs in sub­ur­ban house­holds the world over, van Gogh’s art could still shock some crit­ics with its uncon­ven­tion­al­i­ty. Oth­ers, how­ev­er, showed signs of the enrap­ture­ment that Bonger must have sus­pect­ed would one day be pos­si­ble. Think­ing strate­gi­cal­ly, she pre­ferred to sell few­er pieces for high­er prices, pre­serv­ing the val­ue of his work and lim­it­ing its avail­abil­i­ty on the mar­ket. After her sec­ond hus­band’s death, she redou­bled her ded­i­ca­tion to the art that had become her life’s mis­sion, even trans­lat­ing and pub­lish­ing the hun­dreds of let­ters he’d left behind, most of which were sent to Theo. We’ve heard many artists described as mar­ried to their work, a cliché that applies well enough to Vin­cent van Gogh him­self. But to be mar­ried to one’s broth­er-in-law’s work is a rar­er thing indeed — and some­times a more impor­tant one.

title: Robin F. Williams Suspends the Allure and Horror of Technology in an Endless Loop
description: A nude figure with frazzled hair lies in bed, the sickly colored linens draped across their upper body. Fingertips glowing red as if inflamed, the
body:
A nude figure with frazzled hair lies in bed, the sickly colored linens draped across their upper body. Fingertips glowing red as if inflamed, the character grasps a navy phone and stares catatonically at the screen. A vibrant infinity symbol is superimposed on the scene, emerging as endless loops of energy and mesmerization from the device.
The all-too-relatable portrait is part of a suite of new works by Robin F. Williams capturing the omnipotent techno-dystopia we’re collectively barreling toward. Extrapolating on the ways humanity and machines merge, the Brooklyn-based artist presents a mystical vision of another world infused with pop culture and art history. 
“Merminator” (2026), oil on linen, 60 x 40 inches
“The Merminator,” for example, combines two characters of the ’80s—a cyborg assassin and a Disney princess—to form a metallic bot perched on a stone as it, like Ariel, peers toward a world it presumably longs to be part of and yet won’t be accepted in. 
There’s also “I Am Not a Robot,” a symmetric piece that takes cues in composition and color palette from the spiritualist abstractions of Hilma af Klint. The painting also draws from Boticelli’s “Madonna of the Pomegranate,” which presents the titular fruit as a visual metaphor for the human heart. In Williams’ iteration, though, the subject is the phone, radiating outward in place of the life-giving source.
Under the fitting title Act Natural, the body of work plunges into the uncanny without settling into the strange state of things. The too-sleek, frictionless world the artist portrays exudes the allure of technology alongside the immense horror it elicits.
P·P·O·W presents Act Natural as a pop-up at Frieze’s No. 9 Cork Street in London, where it’s on view through October 24. Explore more of Williams’ work on Instagram.

title: The Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Winners Showcase Nature's Power and Vulnerability
description: Federico Veronesi received the top honor of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year for his poignant black-and-white image of a female elephant
body:
Federico Veronesi received the top honor of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year for his poignant black-and-white image of a female elephant carrying her deceased calf. The portrait represents a rare insight into animals’ habits we have yet to fully understand and demonstrates the power of timing and persistence in photography.
Veronesi had been tracking elephants in the Huab River Valley of Namibia when he encountered some unusual drag marks on the earth. He eventually caught up with the family, and the adult emerged with the calf’s leg wedged between her trunk and tusk.  “Behaviours centering on death have been observed in both Asian and African elephants, including vocalisations, guarding the dead, inspecting and handling bones, and carrying the deceased,” a statement says. “Some researchers suggest these behaviours could indicate an elephant’s journey to understanding death, while others interpret these actions as possible displays of grief.”
Federico Veronesi (Italy), “The Aftermath.” Winner, Wildlife Photographer of the Year and Behaviour: Mammals  category. An elephant carries a dead calf in a rare glimpse into complex animal behaviours
Additional winners include Kutub Uddin’s capture of elegant slime molds, Loren Elliott’s portfolio featuring the coyotes of San Francisco, and Amelie Davis’ portrait of a bee coming in for a landing on a flower in Surrey, England, in the 10 and Under category. “This year’s winning photographs demonstrate the extraordinary power of wildlife photography to help us see nature differently,” says Dr. Doug Gurr, Director of the Natural History Museum. “Together they remind us that every species plays a role in the complex web of life, and why understanding and protecting the natural world has never been more important.”
At 65,403 entries from photographers in 121 countries, this year’s competition saw the largest turnout of submissions in its 62-year history. Categories run the gamut of photojournalism, wetlands, plants and fungi, behavior, portfolios, youth categories, and more. The 100 top images from this year’s contest go on view tomorrow, October 16, at the Natural History Museum in London, where they’ll be exhibited through July 11, 2027. 
Francisco Negroni (Chile), “Warning Sign.” Winner, Photojournalism category. The photographer captures this scene of a dead puma amid the rugged, windswept beauty of Argentine Patagonia
Kutub Uddin (Bangladesh/U.K.), “Tiny Dancers,” from the ‘Secret Worlds’ portfolio. Winner, Portfolio Award. Fine threads, known as capillitium, emerge on the round, yellow-green bodies, which will eventually help disperse reproductive spores
James Lewin (U.K.), “The Meeting Place.” Winner, Animals in their Environment category. A young bull elephant sprays a group of zebra as they congregate in the Kenyan Chyulu Hills
Loren Elliott (U.S.), “On the Outskirts” from the ‘Wily Coyotes of San Francisco’ portfolio. Winner, Photojournalist Story Award. A coyote pads along a trail in Bernal Heights Park, overlooking the city and bay of San Francisco
Agorastos Papatsanis (Greece), “Shedding Light.” Winner, Plants and Fungi category. Ultraviolet light reveals the glowing yellow stems of bonnet mushrooms growing from a decaying log
Anton Sorokin (U.S.), “Protective Pose.” Winner, Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles category. A California newt lays its eggs as it clasps vegetation that already holds another newt’s egg clutch
Alex Visbal (Colombia), “The Great Divide.” Winner, Wetlands: The Bigger Picture category. A single engineered line reshapes an entire wetland
Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas (Germany), “Afternoon Snack,” from the ‘Hidden Depths’ portfolio. Winner, Rising Star Award. A robber fly impales a flesh fly with its needlelike mouthparts

title: 12 Must-Read Books on Textiles and Fiber Art
description:
Guide
                Titles on contemporary Diné weavers, Black American quilting in California, the Bayeux Tapestry, artists i
body:
Guide
                Titles on contemporary Diné weavers, Black American quilting in California, the Bayeux Tapestry, artists including Cecilia Vicuña and Olga de Amaral, and more.
                
        
            A ~patchwork~ of books to read this month (edit Hyperallergic)
    
        
            There’s a reason the lexicon of textiles and fiber lends itself so well to storytelling — we thread the needle, weave the tale, spin the yarn. Writers have reached for these metaphors for centuries because they feel true to life, but artists know they’re also true to craft and its tangled histories. We’ve gathered a few recent books on embroidery, fiber art, weaving, and more that deserve a closer look, from Black Southern quilting and Korean bojagi to Palestinian tatreez and contemporary Diné weaving. Refreshingly, so many of these titles complicate or refuse reductive, familiar frameworks and open up new ways to understand the meditative and political dimensions of textile traditions, moving past the false dichotomy of “craft versus art” and sexist and tired notions of “women’s work.” You might even say these books piece together a new history of textile art, stitch by stitch. —Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor and books editorReparative Craft: Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick as a Textile Artist by Jason Edwards | Duke University Press, 2026I know Eve Sedgwick from her deeply influential work in queer and literary theory, but it had somehow escaped me that she was also an artist. This book, which straddles literary and craft theory, examines her textile art between the mid-1990s and 2000s — the period in which she was also writing Touching Feeling. Some of those same ideas — particularly her preoccupation with Buddhism — can be found in her dreamy textile collages and sculptures meditating on illness, repair, and death. —Lisa Yin ZhangStories in the Seams: A People's History of Black Quilts and Their Makers by Sharbreon Plummer | Chronicle Books, 2026In an opinion piece for Hyperallergic in June, Sharbreon Plummer argued that Black American quilts are inseparable from the inner lives of their makers. Organized into three parts, “memory,” “method,” and “medicine,” Stories in the Seams is the fruit of that pivotal reframing. This compassionate collection of essays, homages, and interviews with Black American quiltmakers centers their interiority as much as their technique. Plummer — who also participated in a roundtable in Routed West, featured in this list as well — traces these quilts’ influence on artists and writers like Romare Bearden and bell hooks. As she writes in her introduction, “Black quilts remind us that healing, connection, and creativity are still possible.” —Lakshmi Rivera Amin

title: Tanya Merrill's Animal Instinct
description:
Pocket Review
								After a move upstate and a newborn, Merrill’s new work responds to the world around her.
body:
Pocket Review
								After a move upstate and a newborn, Merrill’s new work responds to the world around her. 
						
								
																
														
								
						
		
	  		    
        
            Tanya Merrill "A milking cow at Evelyn's dairy" (2026), oil and graphite on linen (all images Gregory Volk/Hyperallergic)
    
		
				
						Two life-changing experiences lie at the heart of the captivating new oil-and-graphite paintings in Tanya Merrill’s exhibition, Land animal, house animal: The artist gave birth to her daughter in June, and her family recently relocated from New York City to upstate New York. In her new environment, Merrill decisively challenges a pervasive anthropocentric worldview that deems humans superior and animals lesser. She foregrounds local animals as sentient beings with their own motivations and desires, including a cat in two terrific paintings, a wide-eyed and inquisitive dairy cow, and the Northern harrier (or marsh hawk) with piercing eyes and luscious gray, white, and black feathers that she frequently observes from her studio (“Marsh hawk,” 2026). This bird painting echoes regional folk art and Audubon. Tanya Merrill "Horse at night" (2026), oil and graphite on linen

title: Artavazd Pelechian’s Distant Connections
description:
Film Review
                Through his “distance montage” technique, the Armenian filmmaker’s masterpieces are built around imp
body:
Film Review
                Through his “distance montage” technique, the Armenian filmmaker’s masterpieces are built around impressions, not stories. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Still from We (1969), directed by Artavazd Pelechian, (all images courtesy New York Film Festival)
    
        
            Artavazd Pelechian said his piece, and his admirers have waited decades for the world to take notice. The Armenian filmmaker, active primarily during the Soviet era, has a concise oeuvre: 13 works, mostly shorts, with two features that barely crack an hour. Aside from 2019’s Nature, he has not released anything since 1994. International recognition came gradually, but it has grown enough that many of his films have received 4K restorations that premiered at different festivals over 2026. Recently, the Pelechian Project was showcased at the New York Film Festival (NYFF), with eight of the director’s restored works in the program.At the storied All-Union State Institute of Cinematography in Moscow in the 1960s, Pelechian and his peers studied the work of titanic Soviet directors like Sergei Eisenstein, Vsevolod Pudovkin, and Dziga Vertov, who shaped cinematography and editing in cinema’s early days. Pelechian deviated from their example, developing an approach he described as “distance montage.” All his movies are montage-based, with intricate shot assemblages unified by distinct themes. Speaking with Scott MacDonald in the 1990s, Pelechian explained the distinction between distance montage and the familiar notion of a montage: In Eisenstein, every element means something. For me, the individual fragments don’t mean anything anymore. Only the whole film has the meaning. … Eisenstein saw editing as a means to get from here to there, [whereas] I see editing as a means for seeing where we are.Still from The Seasons (1975), directed by Artavazd Pelechian
